content: Amoxicillin, also known as amoxycillin, is a moderate-spectrum β-lactam antibiotic that is used to treat bacterial infections caused by susceptible microorganisms. It is often the preferred drug within its class due to its superior absorption when administered orally compared to other β-lactam antibiotics. However, amoxicillin is vulnerable to degradation by β-lactamase-producing bacteria. To counteract this, it is frequently combined with clavulanic acid, which inhibits β-lactamase activity, thereby extending its spectrum of activity. Amoxicillin was developed by Beecham in 1972 and is currently marketed by GlaxoSmithKline under the original trade name Amoxil. The mechanism of action of amoxicillin involves the inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis. Specifically, it prevents the cross-linking of linear peptidoglycan polymer chains, which are a critical component of the cell wall in Gram-positive bacteria. Microbiologically, amoxicillin is effective against a broad range of Gram-positive organisms and a limited range of Gram-negative organisms. Examples of susceptible Gram-negative bacteria include non-β-lactamase-producing strains of Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Neisseria meningitidis, Escherichia coli, Proteus mirabilis, and Salmonella species. However, it is ineffective against penicillinase-producing organisms, such as penicillinase-producing Staphylococcus species, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and Haemophilus influenzae. Other resistant organisms include Serratia marcescens and Citrobacter species. The prevalence of β-lactamase-producing resistant organisms, including E. coli, is increasing. In pediatric cases, doubling the standard dose of amoxicillin has been shown to eradicate intermediately resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae in certain infections. Amoxicillin is available in various formulations, including capsules, tablets, and syrup for oral use, as well as a sodium salt form for intravenous administration. It is one of the most commonly prescribed antibiotics for children. The molecule has three ionizable groups. When combined with clavulanic acid (as potassium clavulanate), amoxicillin's spectrum of activity is expanded to include additional Gram-negative organisms and to overcome bacterial resistance mediated by β-lactamase production. This combination is known as co-amoxiclav (British Approved Name) and is marketed under various proprietary names, such as Augmentin, Clamoxyl, and Amoksiklav. The side effects of amoxicillin are similar to those of other β-lactam antibiotics. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, and fatigue. Allergic reactions to amoxicillin can occur suddenly and may be severe, requiring immediate medical attention. Symptoms of an allergic reaction often begin with changes in mental state, intense itching and rash (commonly starting at the fingertips or groin and spreading rapidly), fever, nausea, and vomiting. Any suspicious symptoms should be taken seriously and addressed promptly. The patent for amoxicillin has expired, and it is now marketed under numerous trade names worldwide, including Actimoxi, Amoxil, Amoksiklav, Curam, Augmentin, and many others.
